To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a router mechanism for identifying and restricting the bandwidth of best effort flows is needed.

the Internet is currently not congested, and that the Internet can continue to function properly without any changes to the current Internet architecture, provided that the current Internet architecture remains unchanged.

(a) the Internet is becoming increasingly congested, (b) this congestion is due to a growing deployment of non TCP friendly applications, (c) the deployment of these applications can lead to congestion collapse, and (d) router based mechanisms are required to identify and restrict these flows in times of high congestion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of router mechanisms that can identify flows using disproportionate bandwidth and regulate the bandwidth of these flows in a way that does not interfere with other flows.
the design and implementation of router mechanisms to regulate the bandwidth of high bandwidth best effort traffic in times of congestion.

the design and deployment of a router based bandwidth regulation scheme that can be used to restrict the bandwidth of flows identified as unresponsive, not TCP friendly or disproportionate bandwidth users.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a flow should be identified for regulation when it is not TCP friendly, is unresponsive, or uses disproportionate bandwidth.
there are a number of approaches for identifying high bandwidth flows, but no single approach can be recommended as being universally superior.
the use of end-to-end congestion control in the transport layer is a necessary but not sufficient condition for congestion control.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of end-to-end congestion control in the best effort Internet is a desirable goal.
the Internet needs a new router mechanism that identifies and limits high bandwidth flows.
the Internet is currently not designed for the best effort traffic that is being generated today, let alone for the best effort services that are envisioned in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the identification of disproportionate bandwidth flows can be achieved with minimal additional overhead.
it is possible to identify flows using disproportionate bandwidth, but not necessarily unresponsive or not TCP friendly flows.
it is possible to design router mechanisms that can effectively regulate the bandwidth of flows that are not TCP friendly, and that these router mechanisms can be implemented with low overhead.
